knowledge_point.title: Computing an Integral Using the Sum Rule

question.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the sum rule, we compute the sum of the integrals of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{3}}}+4\right)\,\mathrm{d}x &= \int \left(\frac{1}{x^{\frac{3}{2}}}+4\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &= \int x^{-\frac{3}{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x+4\int 1\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &= \frac{x^{-\frac{3}{2}+1}}{(-\frac{3}{2}+1)}+4\frac{x^{0+1}}{(0+1)}+C \\ &= -\frac{2}{\sqrt{x}}+4x+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
We know that $y'(t)=-2+t^{6}$.

Applying the sum rule, we compute the sum of the integrals of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \left(-2+t^{6}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t &= \int \left(-2+t^{6}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &= -2\int 1\,\mathrm{d}t+\int t^{6}\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &= -2\frac{t^{0+1}}{(0+1)}+\frac{t^{6+1}}{(6+1)}+C \\ &= -2t+\frac{t^{7}}{7}+C\end{aligned}
$$
